records.sourceFile: Physical preparation of the football player with an intramuscular hamstring tendon tear- clinical perspective with video demonstrations.pdf

paper.citation: Taberner M, Cohen DD. Physical preparation of the football player with an intramuscular hamstring tendon tear: clinical perspective with video demonstrations. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;52(19):1275-1278.
paper.abstract: The article has no abstract. It opens with a case scenario: a Premier League footballer with a proximal intramuscular hamstring tendon injury, rehabilitated over a structured programme and returned to competition in 120 days. The author describes the loading progression and the objective criteria used to progress, and presents the case in an education review with video demonstrations.
paper.tldr: A single Premier League player with a proximal intramuscular hamstring tendon tear was progressed through isometric, loaded, sprint and plyometric phases, using force-platform and NordBord asymmetry and strength criteria. The player returned in 120 days and was injury free for 13 months.
paper.methods: Clinical case description and education review by the treating physical preparation lead. The author reports the exercise progression by phase and the criteria used to progress, including isometric posterior chain peak force asymmetry (under 10%), NordBord eccentric knee flexor strength (500 N, asymmetry under 10%), and graded high-speed running exposure with GPS monitoring. The article is supported by video demonstrations.
paper.findings: The player progressed from isometric holds to loaded and dynamic exercise, then to plyometrics and high-speed running (above 5.5 m/s from week 10). Isometric posterior chain asymmetry was under 10% by week 9, and total peak force reached 300 N in weeks 13 to 14. Before return, NordBord eccentric strength was 500 N, 13% above preseason and above the 350 N risk threshold cited from another study, with under 10% asymmetry. The player reached a new maximal speed during the return-to-play phase, returned to competition at 120 days and was injury free 13 months later.
paper.limitations: One player, with no control group, no formal statistical analysis and no measurement of tendon structure or stiffness. The author states that there is no evidence that the proposed mechanical stimuli (cyclic high strain, tendon stiffness) are delivered or produce the expected adaptations. The 350 N threshold comes from a prospective cohort of elite players and is applied here to an individual. Co-author Cohen is a co-founder and shareholder of a company that makes force platforms and force platform software, and the progression criteria rely on force-platform testing.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use a phased, criteria-based progression for proximal intramuscular tendon injuries: isometric loading first, then loaded and eccentric work, then plyometrics and graded high-speed running, with progression tied to force asymmetry and NordBord strength. These gates come from one case and the author's judgement, so they are a framework to test in the local setting rather than a validated protocol.
paper.athleteDev: A phased progression from isometric to plyometric and high-speed running work, with asymmetry and strength gates, got one elite player back to full training. The case shows a feasible sequence, not a proven effect on performance, speed or re-injury rates in other players.
paper.rtp: The single case returned to competition at 120 days with NordBord eccentric strength of 500 N and under 10% asymmetry, and stayed injury free for 13 months. One case cannot set return-to-play timelines or criteria for other players, and it does not address surgical decisions for intramuscular tendon injury, which the author notes is unresolved.

records.sourceFile: Post-Operative Rehabilitation and Return to Sport Criteria Following Distal Biceps Tendon Rupture Surgery.pdf

paper.citation: Phelps BM, Birnbrich A, Singer W, Bohle K, George A, Jack RA II. Post-Operative Rehabilitation and Return to Sport Criteria Following Distal Biceps Tendon Rupture Surgery. JSES Int. 2025.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined rehabilitation protocols and return-to-sport criteria after surgical repair of distal biceps tendon rupture. Five studies (268 patients) met inclusion criteria, and the authors found no consensus on return-to-sport criteria. All included studies used time-based criteria, and none reported objective or functional measures.
paper.tldr: Five studies on distal biceps repair all used time-based return-to-sport timelines, and none used objective or functional criteria. The review supports the need for a validated protocol but does not provide one.
paper.methods: Systematic review reported in accordance with PRISMA and described as registered in PROSPERO (no registration number is printed). Five databases were searched from inception to March 2022 for English-language studies of operatively treated distal biceps rupture with at least 12 months follow-up. Methodological quality was scored with the modified Coleman Methodology Score, and return-to-sport criteria were scored on a 0 to 4 scale.
paper.findings: Five studies (268 patients; 206 male, 1 female, 61 sex not reported; three of the five mixed athletes and non-athletes) were included, with a mean modified Coleman score of 61.6 (fair). All five used range of motion followed by strengthening in a multiphase program, four (80%) used cast or splint immobilization for 2 to 5 weeks, and three (60%) used supervised physical therapy. All five gave a recommended return-to-sport timeline, but none reported objective, subjective or specific measurement criteria, and the authors report an overall return-to-sport rate of 146/171 (85%) across the four studies that gave one.
paper.limitations: The review includes only five studies, all level 3 or 4, with fair methodological quality, and patient-reported outcomes were not pooled; sport and competition level were unreported in most studies. The 146/171 rate cannot be fully rebuilt: the three studies with printed counts give 123/138, and the fourth (Yetter) reports only 70% returning without difficulty with no sample size printed. The Discussion cites an 86% same-level return for Rantanen's competitive lifters and overhead athletes, which does not appear in the Results (14/15, 93%, same level). This is a journal pre-proof, and the PROSPERO registration number is not printed.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not treat any single timeline in these studies as a validated return-to-sport standard, because the authors found only time-based criteria and timelines that varied from 8 weeks to 6 months. The review describes multiphase programs of range of motion followed by strengthening, which the authors report in all included studies. The authors recommend a future checklist of objective and subjective criteria, which the included studies do not provide.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not measure performance outcomes. Return-to-sport rates varied by study, with 40/61 (65.6%) returning to the same or higher intensity in Gowd et al and 14/15 (93%) returning to the same level in Rantanen et al. Inference: this suggests that some athletes may not return to their prior performance level, but the review did not measure performance.
paper.rtp: This review is directly relevant to return to sport but cannot set a readiness standard. It found no objective strength or range-of-motion thresholds for clearance, and its rehabilitation timelines are time-based only.

records.sourceFile: Post-operative protein supplementation following orthopaedic surgery - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: George A, Holderread BM, Lambert BS, Harris JD, McCulloch PC. Post-operative protein supplementation following orthopaedic surgery: A systematic review. Sports Medicine and Health Science. 2024;6:16-24.
paper.abstract: This systematic review asked whether oral protein or amino acid supplementation reduces muscle atrophy or improves outcomes after orthopaedic surgery. Fourteen RCTs (611 patients) covering ACL reconstruction, hip and knee arthroplasty and hip fracture surgery were included. The authors conclude that supplementation reduced post-operative muscle atrophy and often went with better function, but call for standardized, population-specific regimens.
paper.tldr: Across 14 small post-surgical RCTs, mostly in older arthroplasty and hip fracture patients, protein or amino acid supplements were reported to limit thigh muscle atrophy. Only three trials involved ACL reconstruction, with mixed strength results, so the evidence for athletes is thin.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, registered in PROSPERO (number not printed). MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in April 2021 for RCTs of protein or amino acid regimens to counter muscle atrophy after orthopaedic surgery, with two independent reviewers. Quality was rated with the Modified Coleman Methodology Score, and results were summarized narratively because protocols, measures and outcomes were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis.
paper.findings: The authors report less muscle atrophy measured by thigh cross-sectional area with supplementation, most marked at the final follow-up week in 11 of 14 studies, and improved functional measures in 8 of 14, with no significant increase in side effects. In ACLR, Holm et al (n=26, milk protein plus carbohydrate) found greater quadriceps cross-sectional area and strength, Kim et al (n=30, open trial, 40 g whey per day vs no supplement) found greater isokinetic strength at 12 weeks, and Laboute et al (n=45, leucine) found greater thigh circumference but no improvement in strength recovery.
paper.limitations: Mean Coleman scores were fair for ACLR and TKA (55) and poor for THA (46) and hip fracture (44), all 14 regimens differed, follow-up averaged about 8 weeks, and physical therapy was not standardized. Only one ACLR trial recorded habitual protein intake, and muscle mass was measured by thigh cross-sectional area or circumference rather than DEXA. The conclusion that supplementation was beneficial across all surgeries sits alongside a null ACLR strength result (Laboute) and a THA trial with strength but no muscle-mass or functional benefit (Ferrando).
paper.practicalImplications: For athletes after ACL reconstruction, the evidence is three small trials with different products, so it does not establish a dose, product or timing. The authors note that ACLR patients are often young athletes whose baseline protein intake may already be high, so any supplement plan should start from the athlete's habitual intake. The arthroplasty and hip fracture results come from older patients and may not transfer to athletes.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not measure sport performance. Its ACLR trials report quadriceps size and isokinetic strength over 2.7 to 12 weeks of rehabilitation only.
paper.rtp: Time to return to sport was a planned secondary outcome, but no return-to-sport results are reported. The review can inform nutrition support during early ACLR rehabilitation, not clearance timing or criteria.

records.sourceFile: Proprioception and Central Nervous Excitability - Implications for Return-to-Play in Athletes with Ligament or Meniscal Injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Okayama Y, Daikuya S. Proprioception and Central Nervous Excitability: Implications for Return-to-Play in Athletes with Ligament or Meniscal Injuries. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2025;20(8):1122-1130.
paper.abstract: Twenty-one female university basketball players, including six with a prior knee ligament or meniscal injury who were cleared to return to play, held 25% of maximal knee extension torque under visual and verbal feedback. Long-latency reflexes (LLR) in the opponens pollicis were recorded during the hold. Visual feedback produced a higher torque median frequency in uninjured legs and a higher LLR amplitude ratio in previously injured knees, which the authors read as greater central nervous system involvement.
paper.tldr: In a small group of female basketball players, visual feedback during a sustained knee torque hold changed the torque pattern in uninjured legs and the reflex response in previously injured knees. With six injured knees and a heterogeneous injury group, this is a research signal, not a return-to-play test.
paper.methods: Case-control observational study of 21 female university basketball players: 15 without knee injury (both legs, 30 legs) and 6 with ligament or meniscal injury and surgical or conservative management (6 injured knees). Participants held 25% of maximal isometric knee extension torque for 60 s on a Biodex dynamometer under visual feedback or verbal feedback with eyes closed, and the median frequency of the torque curve was calculated. Opponens pollicis LLR was evoked by 16 single pulses per condition at 120% of maximal M-wave intensity, and conditions were compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
paper.findings: In uninjured legs (n = 30), visual feedback gave a higher torque median frequency than verbal feedback (0.38 +/- 0.23 vs 0.22 +/- 0.12 Hz, p < 0.001), and no LLR measure differed significantly. In previously injured knees (n = 6), the LLR/Mmax amplitude ratio was higher with visual feedback (0.04 +/- 0.03 vs 0.03 +/- 0.03, p = 0.039), but torque median frequency did not differ (0.35 +/- 0.32 vs 0.19 +/- 0.11 Hz, p = 0.173). In the one athlete who had not returned to sport on schedule, descriptive values showed greater torque median frequency and lower LLR/Mmax, with no statistical testing.
paper.limitations: Six injured knees and 15 uninjured participants is a very small sample, and the injury group mixes ACL, PCL, MCL and meniscal injuries, surgical and conservative management, and 5 months to 4 years since injury. Each group was analysed only as a within-leg visual versus verbal comparison; injured and uninjured legs were never compared statistically, and the dominant versus non-dominant comparison named in the abstract was not possible according to the discussion. Only the LLR amplitude ratio differed significantly in injured knees, so the abstract's conclusion that visual feedback enhances motor adjustment in athletes with previous injuries is stronger than the statistics, and the suggestions about rehabilitation feedback were not tested.
paper.practicalImplications: Feedback type (visual or verbal) changed torque control in uninjured female basketball players during an isometric knee hold, so it can affect what a single control test measures. This study does not show whether visual feedback helps athletes after ligament or meniscal injury, so staff should not use the LLR result as a readiness cut-off or change rehabilitation feedback on this basis alone.
paper.athleteDev: In this test, feedback type changed torque control in uninjured female basketball players, which may matter when a control or strength test is used with athletes. The study does not show that such a test improves performance or training outcomes.
paper.rtp: The authors suggest the method may aid return-to-sport decisions, but the study has no return-to-sport or re-injury outcomes and only one athlete had not returned. It should not be used as a clearance tool until prospective studies link LLR or torque-control measures to later re-injury or performance.
